title: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry: Chirality Abounds
body_text: Now that I’m back here in the ol’ blogging salt mine, I need to catch up with this year’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry. I generally do this on the morning of the award, but that wasn’t possible this year. It’s a very interesting topic, though, and I certainly don’t want to pass it up. As usual, the basic explanation from the Nobel committee is here, and the more advanced one is here, and as usual they have done an excellent job with these. It has to do with chirality (“handedness”), which is simultaneously a very easy concept to grasp and a very tricky one. That changeover tends to correlate with how long you spend thinking about the idea! Everyone has experienced chirality in the form of commonly encountered items like shoes and gloves that exist in non-superimposable mirror-image forms, but as chemists well appreciate, this phenomenon goes all the way down to the molecular level. And in general, the same symmetry-based conditions apply there as in macroscopic objects. One simple rule is that if an object has a “plane of symmetry” in it then it does not have this chiral character. That’s why a shoe comes in right-handed and left-handed forms (enantiomers, in the lingo) while (for example) a pencil or a can of beans does not. The latter two have down-the-middle planes of symmetry as indeed do many objects, but you do have to look closely: a car might appear symmetrical from the front if you’re just looking at the outside (twinned headlights, etc.) but the steering wheel end up on one side or the other depending on whether you’re buying a car in (for example) the UK or the US, and that makes them right-handed or left-handed as well. For biomolecules, the nature of the single-bonded carbon atom brings chirality up very quickly. Carbon in that state has bonds that point out in a tetrahedral arrangement, and if all four of them have different substituents on them, you have a “chiral center”. (If any two are the same, such as two hydrogens and two other groups, then you can draw a plane of symmetry and that carbon no longer has chiral character). As it happens, a great many of the basic molecules of living systems have such chiral carbons in them, most prominently amino acids (once they’re more complicated than glycine) and carbohydrates. And famously, living cells - every living cell of every creature on this planet - use particular “handedness” for each of those. There are many nomenclature systems to distinguish these, but suffice it to say that proteins in living cells are overwhelmingly made up of the so-called “L” amino acids and the carbohydrates in there are overwhelmingly in the “D” series. Since so much of the chemistry of life depends on the recognition of chemical shapes and surfaces by other molecules, it makes sense that things would be largely “homochiral” to make such recognition more certain, and indeed as amino acids, proteins, carbohydrates, and polysaccharides are produced in living systems their enzyme-catalyzed synthesis (accomplished by enzymes that are themselves made up of chiral amino acids) enforces these preferences. But how did we get to this situation? And why did we end up with the handedness preferences that we have? These questions have been bothering chemists ever since chirality was worked out in the late 1800s, and we still have no final answers to those questions. It’s possible that we’re just seeing frozen accidents in the preference for L-amino acids and D-sugars and that it could just as easily have gone the other way a few billion years ago, or there might be subtle reasons why these series ended up being more likely. A long list of those have been proposed over the years. Something happened, though, for sure, because “abiotic” synthesis of such molecules (non-enzymatic, from nonliving systems) gives you no preference at all, perfect 50/50 splits that are known in the business as “racemic mixtures”. If you do a Urey-Miller experiment or some variation thereof and hit a mixture of simple chemical starting materials with heat, electric sparks, ultraviolet light and so on, you will get all sorts of interesting gunk, including plenty of amino acids and simple carbohydrates. These things are quite easy to form! But they are 50/50 mixes with no “handedness” to them. The same goes when you analyze carbon-rich meteorite samples. These too have amino acids, carbohydrates, even the nucleobases found in DNA and RNA (which by themselves are flat and thus do not have chirality). The basic molecules of life are everywhere in the universe! But any of them with chiral character are invariably 50/50 racemates. Whereas in actual life-as-we-know it they are very, very much not. How do you get chiral life from an achiral soup? The work of this year’s Nobel winners presents a possible answer. We of course don’t know if it’s the answer, but it was a great discovery to find that such results were even possible. One of the things the Nobel writeup emphasizes is that the possibility behind this work was actually raised in 1953 by Frederick Charles Frank, who noted that one could imagine some compound that served as a chemical catalyst for production of more molecules like itself, but not for its mirror-image enantiomer. In true British fashion his paper said that “A laboratory demonstration may not be impossible”. It took decades to show that he was correct! Simple autocatalysis happens reasonably often in chemical systems, and asymmetric catalysts are also very much a thing (and have indeed been the subject of Nobels of their own over the years). But asymmetric autocatalysis of the sort envisioned by Frank had to wait until the work of Henri Kagan in the mid-80s and Kenso Soai in the early 90s. Their results showed that “nonlinear effects” could indeed be realized in this area - if you started with a catalyst that was (say) 55/45 in its balance of enantiomers, you would classically have thought that the product(s) you got from the reaction would be (at best) 55/45 themselves. But not always! Careful attention to the compounds involved can lead you to systems where one enantiomer really does favor the formation of more of itself, and you get enantiomeric excesses in the product of well past what you started with. The Advanced Information takes you through the detailed background, which was filled in over time by various research groups. The complexes formed between such catalytic molecules and the starting materials in the reaction mixture can have different reactivities, with one of them being more likely to lead to a product molecule than the other. There are a lot of variations to work out, depending on how many molecules are participating in these complexes, what the different reactivities are along the way, and what the equilibrium constants are between all the possible species, but carefully lining things up can indeed provide chiral amplification. A lot of people have put a lot of effort into these systems - it turns out that these reaction rates and equilibria can and do change as the reactions go on and use up more starting material (i.e., form more product) and you can then get all kinds of results at different time points. As you’d imagine, the best situations are when a particular molecule not only catalyzes its own formation, but actively interferes with the formation of the other enantiomer, but that’s a situation that require careful tuning on its own. That’s where Soai’s group provided a series of striking results, eventually demonstrating that it was possible to take a catalyst that was just barely tilted towards one enantiomer and have it produce material that was over 99:1 in the end! Many chemists of earlier generations (although not Charles Frederick Frank or those who had understood his proposal) would have probably told you that this was just not possible. But it is! Such systems are very rare, but it’s extraordinary that they exist at all. The exact structural details of how these manage to work have been the subject of active investigation for years, with layer after layer of subtle points about the nature of the actual catalytic species. But the more common examples of enhanced excess chirality are actively sought for by industrial chemists for making chiral molecules (as indeed many pharmaceuticals are). Getting higher enantiomeric excess in your product than anything you put into the reaction still feels like a magic trick to most of us in synthetic organic chemistry, and it can be a great help in making an overall synthetic sequence more feasible. Does these sorts of results explain the origins of biological chirality? As mentioned above, not yet - and since these events took place eons ago, it may never be possible to completely resolve the question. For one thing, you’d have to assume that any such reactions would have been taking place in aqueous solution, and so far, that’s not what has been demonstrated in the lab (as far as I know). But knowing that chiral amplification is a real process has changed the game, for sure. Knowing your right hand from your left seems easy, but knowing where “right” and “left” come from in the first place and how you might get there is indeed Nobel-worthy work.
